workbench.title: Workbench
workbench.brief: Workbench is Gusto’s internal design system — React components, colors, typography, patterns, and all the visual assets common to Gusto’s brand. I was part of the team of designers and engineers who planned and built it from scratch. I built and owned the documentation site itself — which was formerly public, though it’s now internal-only — as the source of truth for the system, with extensive documentation for Gusto’s ~500 designers and engineers, including a monthly newsletter.
workbench.scope: System work: research > API design > accessibility > build. Documentation site: most of the design > content writing > build > deploy.

images.alt: Screenshot of the Workbench getting started page for designers
images.caption: “Getting Started” pages introduce users to the system, tailored to either designers (Figma-based) or engineers (code-based), aided by Loom videos.

images.alt: Screenshot of the Workbench components landing page
images.caption: An extensive collection of React components was available, all thoroughly considered by both design and engineering to ensure they were fit for purpose, accessible, responsive, and performant.

images.alt: Screenshot showing the anatomy of some Workbench form components
images.caption: Documentation for each component — in this case, a collection of form components — included an anatomy graphic to help designers and engineers speak the same language.

images.alt: Screenshot of accessibility notes written for the Workbench Timeline component
images.caption: Each component went through extensive consideration for accessibility; those decisions were thoroughly explained in documentation to educate designers and engineers on the thought process behind the decisions and instructions on how to properly implement the component.

images.alt: Screenshot of the Workbench Timeline component documentation page
images.caption: Each component has a tabbed interface aimed at different purposes: the “Usage” tab explains the why/what/how behind the component, and the “Implementation” tab explains how to use it, including code samples, prop tables, accessibility guidelines, and testing suggestions.

james-button.title: James Button Oboe
james-button.summary: A personal website for a classical oboe musician.
james-button.brief: A web presence for San Francisco Symphony’s Associate Principal Oboist to establish a brand and to promote audition coaching and guest performance work. The color palette is largely drawn from sampling the hero image and features high-legibility typography, an integrated event calendar, and a custom audio player for his excerpts.
james-button.scope: Full scope: Design, UX, content strategy, technical SEO → build → launch.
james-button.status: Live and actively driving client referrals.

beeline.title: The Beeline
beeline.summary: A showcase of road biking routes in San Francisco.
beeline.brief: A streamlined, app-style cycling dashboard built for SF-based riders to filter and explore favorite routes without marketing clutter or unnecessary link-drilling. The name Beeline was inspired by the winding trail a bee leaves looping through the air—similar to the way bike routes weave around the Bay Area. The bold, playful design references the colors of a bee.
beeline.scope: Full scope: Design, content → build → launch).
beeline.status: v1 is live. Next phase: re-riding routes to catalog explicit points of interest like water stops, lunch spots, and viewpoints.

lindsay-flowers.title: Lindsay Flowers Oboe
lindsay-flowers.summary: A personal website for oboe musician Lindsay Flowers.
lindsay-flowers.brief: A web presence for University of Wisconsin–Madison oboe instructor Lindsay Flowers to drive student recruitment and promote professional services. Features a traditional, elegant aesthetic tailored for classical music audiences.
lindsay-flowers.scope: Full scope: Design, UX, style guide, content strategy, technical SEO → build → launch.
lindsay-flowers.status: Figma design complete; development in Astro is underway while Lindsay finalizes the site content.

tails.title: Tails
tails.summary: A digital library of my personal cocktail collection.
tails.brief: A clean, ad-free mobile cocktail recipe catalog designed to keep focus on drink preparation rather than dismissing popups. I call it Tails, as in cocktails (hold for applause). There’s relatively little interactivity, so React—and by extension, Next.js—felt like overkill, so I built it in Astro instead.
tails.scope: Full scope: Design, content → build → launch).
tails.status: v1 is live. Planned enhancements: search functionality, favorites, and further mobile UI polish.
